migrationNotes: Spine: watch one patch of water lilies on a 20 square metre pond. It doubles every day while nothing holds it back, slows as the pond fills, levels off near the pond's size, and then the limit itself moves when half the pond is filled in. Births and deaths are counted along the way.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-population-limits-1 and -closed-why. Doubling from 10 is asked by the hook (-hook) and the skill check (-8); a closed population is explained on the screen about births and deaths.

lesson.title: Limits to growth

lead.text: Follow the lily patch day by day. Today it covers 1 square metre. After one day it covers 2, after two days 4 and after three days 8. The patch grows by the same proportion every day, and that proportion is its growth rate. Doubling is a growth rate of 100% a day, because the patch gains as much area as it already had.

afterFigure.text: Look at what the numbers do. The patch adds 1 square metre on the first day, 2 on the second and 4 on the third. The growth rate stays the same, but the amount added gets bigger every day, because there is more patch to do the growing. The figure sets it beside a patch that simply gains 1 square metre a day, which falls behind. A doubling population creeps along at first and then takes off. It cannot go on for ever in a pond of fixed size, since the patch cannot cover more than the whole pond.

lead.text: Carry on doubling from where the figure stops.
The patch cannot go on doubling once the pond is nearly covered. Think about what the lilies need and how much of it there is for each leaf as the pond fills.

reveal.text: Compare your prediction with the figure. The patch still grows, but each day adds less than the day before.

lead.text: Look at the real pond's curve. For the first three days the lilies double, adding 1, 2 and 4 square metres. Over the next three days the patch adds 5, 4 and 2, a little less each time, and it levels off close to the pond's area of 20 square metres. The leaves are crowding one another for light and space, so new shoots find it harder to start and old leaves die more often. The same happens in every population. As numbers rise, each individual has less food, space or shelter to itself, and the competition lowers births or raises deaths, and often does both.

afterFigure.text: The size of population that a habitat can keep supporting is its carrying capacity. For the lilies in this pond it is set mostly by space, about 20 square metres. For deer it might be set by the winter food supply. A population that grows fast at first and then levels off near its carrying capacity traces an S-shaped curve, which biologists call logistic growth.

lead.text: Use the biologist's name for the size that the lily curve levels off near.

The curve is a record of numbers, and the numbers change for two main reasons. Individuals are born, and individuals die. To keep the count simple we use a closed population, one that nothing joins or leaves except through birth and death, so no animals arrive from elsewhere and none walk away. The difference between the births and the deaths in a period is the population's net change.

Take a closed population of 50, with 12 births and 7 deaths in a season. The net change is 12 − 7 = 5, so the population rises to 50 + 5 = 55. If deaths outnumbered births the net change would be negative and the population would fall. If births and deaths were equal, the population would stay the same size even though individuals were being born and dying all the time. That balance is what we see at the carrying capacity.
Count what the population gains and what it loses over one interval.
Find the net change first, then apply it to the starting size.

The carrying capacity of a habitat is not a fixed number. It depends on the resources the habitat offers, and those can change. Suppose half of the pond is filled in to make a path. The lilies now have only 10 square metres to spread across, and the same patch that once levelled off near 20 levels off near 10 instead. The carrying capacity of the pond for lilies has halved.

afterFigure.text: The same goes for other species. A habitat has a different carrying capacity for each species, because species need different things. Space for lilies says nothing about how many herons or fish the same pond can feed, since each depends on other resources. So a carrying capacity belongs to one species in one habitat under particular conditions, and when the conditions change, it changes with them.

lead.text: A population of grazing animals was near its limit when a drought cut the food supply.

steps.headline: What a smooth curve leaves out

lead.text: The S-shaped curve is a model: a simplified picture that keeps the main idea and leaves out the detail. It is useful because it shows why growth slows and roughly where it levels off. Real populations do not follow it exactly. Weather changes the food supply from year to year, disease can sweep through a crowded population, and chance decides which individuals happen to breed. A real count wobbles around the smooth line, and a population can overshoot its carrying capacity for a time before it falls back.

The curve explains the general pattern. To know what one particular population is doing you have to count it. A model that gets the shape right is doing its job, and it is asking too much of it to expect every rise and dip.

lesson.orientation: Compare proportional growth with resource-limited growth and changing carrying capacity.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The last lesson showed how little energy passes up a food chain, which means a pond can feed only so much life. This lesson asks what that limit does to a single kind of organism growing in it.

A pond covers 20 square metres. Today a single square metre of its surface is covered with water lilies, which float their leaves on the water and spread by sending out new shoots. Under good conditions the patch doubles its area every day. A group of one kind of living thing in one place is a population, and the lily patch is a population that is easy to follow, because its size is simply the area it covers.

For the first few days the patch hardly shows against the whole pond. Following it day by day shows how a population grows when nothing holds it back, what finally does hold it back, and how to keep count when individuals are born and die.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell unlimited growth from limited growth, and work out how births and deaths change a population.

recap.keyIdea: With nothing to hold it back a population grows faster each round, but limited resources slow it near the carrying capacity, and that limit changes with conditions.

blocks.text: You doubled a lily patch until it would have outgrown its pond, and watched the real patch level off near 20 square metres. You found a population's size from its births and deaths. You also saw half the pond filled in lower the limit to about 10 square metres.

recap.nextHook: Everything in these two lessons rested on numbers that someone measured. The next lesson asks how to test a claim with measurements, using two plants and a bag of fertiliser.

questions.prompt: A population starts at 10 and doubles each round. What is it after three rounds?
questions.onCorrect: 80. Each round doubles the last, so the increases grow larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 10 each round. Each round doubles instead.
That is the count after only two rounds.

questions.prompt: A population grows quickly at first and then levels off. What is the name for the size of population that its habitat can keep supporting?
hints: Competition for resources lowers net growth near this level.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity reflects the population supported by those conditions.

questions.onCorrect: Carrying capacity. Growth levels off near the size the habitat can support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are rates. The question asks for the size the habitat can support.

questions.prompt: A closed population has 12 births and 12 deaths in one interval. What is its net change?
hints: There is no migration in this closed population.
Subtract the deaths from the births.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 − 12 = 0, although individuals were born and died.

questions.onCorrect: Zero. Births and deaths balance, so the size is steady even though individuals come and go.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the births and deaths together. Deaths take away from the population.
That is the births alone. Take the deaths away.

questions.prompt: After a drought reduces the food supply, what may happen to the carrying capacity?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying capacity depends on environmental resources and conditions.

choices.label: It becomes the same for every species

questions.onCorrect: It can decrease. Carrying capacity depends on conditions, so it is not a fixed number.

misconceptions.feedback: It depends on resources, and a drought changes them.
Each species needs different resources, so each has its own limit.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 70, with 16 births and 9 deaths. What is its final size?
questions.onCorrect: 77. Net change is births minus deaths, added to the starting size.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the deaths. Subtract them.
That swaps the two: it subtracts the births and adds the deaths.

questions.prompt: Does a smooth logistic curve predict every fluctuation in a wild population?
hints: Identify the processes the model omits.

acceptedIdeas: No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The curve is a simplified model; real populations can fluctuate or overshoot.

choices.label: Only for populations above one million
No, weather, interactions and chance can cause departures

questions.onCorrect: No. The curve is a simplified model, and weather, interactions and chance shift real numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: A smooth curve leaves out weather, disease and chance.
Population size does not make a model exact.

questions.prompt: A closed population starts at 120, with 30 births and 45 deaths. What is its final size?
questions.onCorrect: 105. Deaths outnumbered births, so the population fell.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the deaths. Subtract them.
That adds the deaths. Deaths reduce the population.
That swaps the two: it adds the deaths and subtracts the births.

questions.prompt: A population of 6 doubles every round with no limit. How many are there after four rounds?
questions.onCorrect: 96. Four doublings multiply the starting number by 16.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 6 each round. Doubling multiplies instead.
That is the count after only three rounds.

questions.prompt: A pond is 20 square metres. A patch of lilies covers 1 square metre today and doubles its area every day, with nothing to stop it. On which day from today does the patch first cover more than 20 square metres?
hints: Write the area for each day: it doubles every time.
Keep doubling until the area passes the pond's size.
Check the area on day four, then on the day after.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The area is 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 on days 0 to 4, and 32 on day 5, which is over 20.

questions.onCorrect: Day 5. Doubling is slow at first and then very fast, because each increase is bigger than the last.

misconceptions.feedback: On that day the patch covers 16 square metres, which is still under 20.
That is the pond's size in square metres. The question asks for a day.

questions.prompt: As the pond becomes crowded, what happens to the patch's growth each day: does it speed up, stay the same or slow down?
hints: Think about food and space as numbers rise.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Crowding lowers births or raises deaths, so growth slows.

questions.onCorrect: It slows down. Crowding cuts births or raises deaths, so each round adds less.

misconceptions.feedback: More individuals share the same food and space, which makes things harder, not easier.
Competition changes births and deaths as numbers rise, so the growth does not stay fixed.

questions.prompt: Why is this population called closed?
hints: Think about what could change the number besides births and deaths.

acceptedIdeas: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A closed population has no migration, so only births and deaths change its size.

choices.label: Individuals enter or leave only by birth and death
It lives in a closed jar

questions.onCorrect: No one arrives or leaves. Only births and deaths change the size.

misconceptions.feedback: Deaths do occur. A closed population just has no migration.
Closed describes movement of individuals, not the container.
